root.note: Dictionaries trace Italian balcone to a Germanic word for ‘beam’; the Italian form with -one is an augmentative.

history: A balcony starts with a beam. Germanic languages had a word for a big wooden beam, *balko, and Italian borrowed it in the Middle Ages as balco, a beam or scaffold. With the augmentative ending -one, ‘big’, the word gave balcone: a platform carried out from a wall on beams. In the 1600s English borrowed balcony from Italian, and French took balcon. English balk, as in ‘the horse balked’, is a distant relative, and so is German Balken. If you rent a flat in Italy, the listing will say balcone for a small outside space with a railing, and terrazzo for a larger one. A veranda is closed in by windows.
historyEinfach: Balcone comes from a Germanic word for ‘beam’. A balcone is a platform held up on beams. English took the word from Italian in the 1600s. German Balken (beam) is a relative.

elsewhere.text: English borrowed balcony from Italian in the 1600s. The stress shifted, from bal-CO-ne in Italian to BAL-co-ny in English.
